name: Longs Peak and Mount Meeker via the Loft

legs.route: Loft Couloir, then the short walk to the summit from the top of the Loft
Clark's Arrow downclimb and Keplinger's Couloir to the Homestretch
legs.connect: Back from the Meeker summit to the top of the Loft, drop down the far side to the cairn marking the Clark's Arrow downclimb, cross to Keplinger's Couloir and join the Homestretch.

how: Climb the Loft couloir from the Boulderfield trail to the notch at its top, then detour to Meeker, which adds roughly an hour. Return to the Loft and descend its back side by a class 3-4 downclimb, then take Keplinger's Couloir (loose scree, some ice or steep snow high up) to reach the Homestretch and the Longs summit plateau. Early season wants an ice axe and crampons for the Loft snowfield and the traverse near the top of Keplinger's.
descent: Come down the standard Keyhole route: Ledges, Narrows and Trough, then through the Keyhole and back to the Boulderfield trail. This is the same descent as a plain Longs day, but you reach it far later and more tired.
logistics: Start in the dark, since the full day runs 12 to 17 hours and 14.5 miles with about 6,000 ft of gain. All of it is above treeline, so storm timing matters; turn back if the Loft or Clark's Arrow is wet or icy. Check park rules for the Longs summit season.
notes: Both reports go Loft up, Meeker first, Clark's Arrow + Keplinger's to Longs, Keyhole down. Meeker summit-block difficulty: easy class 3 in one report; Clark's Arrow downclimb class 3-4 (higher kept). Reverse order (Longs first) not confirmed so omitted.

name: Arapaho Peaks Traverse (South and North Arapaho)

legs.route: Arapaho Glacier Trail to the saddle, then the southeast slopes
Connecting ridge north (class 3-4)
legs.connect: Follow the ridge crest, or just west of it, for roughly three quarters of a mile, passing a slabby section and a short downclimb.

how: From the trailhead, take the Arapaho Pass trail to the old mine, then the glacier trail to the saddle and scramble boulders to South Arapaho. The ridge to North Arapaho is mostly class 3 with a crux of class 4 on a short slab or downclimb; the west side is less exposed and offers escapes. Some parties carry a short rope or leave one at the crux.
descent: Retrace the ridge and the route over South Arapaho, or drop back to the saddle where possible. It is out and back, with no loop and no shuttle.
logistics: Roughly 9 to 10 miles and 3,500 to 3,900 ft of gain. The lot fills early on weekends and the access road is rough. A wilderness permit is needed for overnight use. Best from June through September; lingering snow sits just below the North Arapaho summit early in the season.
notes: Distance varies by page (8.3 to 10.4 mi); gain 3,500 to 3,900 ft. Crux ranges from 3rd class (one solo report) to class 4 / possibly 5 (slab); higher kept. Some guides show it as a one-way from the saddle then back over South Arapaho.

name: Castle Peak and Conundrum Peak

legs.route: Northeast Ridge from Montezuma Basin
South Ridge from the Castle-Conundrum saddle
legs.connect: Walk down Castle's ridge about 440 ft to the saddle, then follow the well-trodden ridge up to Conundrum (the true summit is the second, higher point).

how: Climb Castle by its northeast ridge, which has a few short scrambles. From the summit drop to the saddle, then gain the roughly 250 ft to Conundrum on a loose but straightforward ridge. The pair is treated as an easy double, mostly class 2 with brief harder moves on Castle.
descent: Two ways down: use the saddle shortcut from the saddle into the upper basin (steeper and looser than the normal route, snowy early in the season), or climb back over Castle. The shortcut saves the extra climb.
logistics: The upper trailhead is reached by a rough road, so many parties start lower and walk the road. Bring an axe and traction if snow remains on the headwall or saddle slopes, which can hold snow well into summer. Leave early; afternoon storms build quickly.
notes: One report descends the Conundrum couloir (loose then snow) instead of the saddle shortcut; the other uses the shortcut. Castle route read on 14ers as Difficult Class 2. Total about 8 miles and 3,350 ft from the upper lot in one report.

name: Wetterhorn Peak and Uncompahgre Peak

legs.route: Southeast Ridge from the Matterhorn Creek trailhead
Southeast ridge / standard route, joined by a cross-country link
legs.connect: Descend the Wetterhorn trail to the boulder field, cross the stream on a faint stock trail, follow the Matterhorn saddle stock driveway and cross the Cimarron headwaters to join the Uncompahgre trail.

how: Do Wetterhorn first: it is the harder peak (class 3 crux headwall and ledges) and the closer one, so it is banked early. The link to Uncompahgre is a long, mostly trail-and-tundra traverse of about nine miles between the two summits, ending with class 2 ridge scrambling with a few false summits. Plan on 8 to 11 hours.
descent: Return the way you came, via the high stock trail to the Matterhorn saddle and down to the trailhead. There is no loop; the direct line from the saddle to the Wetterhorn trail is easy but hard to spot.
logistics: About 17 miles and 6,000 to 6,400 ft of gain from the Matterhorn Creek trailhead. Summer window runs July through September; a forest parking permit and a high-clearance vehicle may be needed at the upper lot. Start before dawn for the afternoon storms.
notes: Matterhorn Peak (13er) can be added per CMC and a search snippet, but no page read in full gave route detail, so it is not a leg. One 14ers report notes a guidebook does Uncompahgre first (to allow a bailout); the reports read do Wetterhorn first. Gain 5,600 to 6,400 ft by source.

name: Tenmile Traverse (Peak 1 to Peak 10)

legs.route: Trail from Rainbow Lake trailhead to the ridge; Mount Royal and Mount Victoria are optional earlier summits
Ridge south, about half a mile from Peak 1
legs.connect: Follow the crest over the rocky Dragon's Tail area, bypassing the worst towers on the west side.

legs.route: Ridge scramble past Peak 2
legs.connect: Continue the narrow crest; route-finding is trickiest between Peaks 2 and 3.

legs.route: Exposed ridge scramble with knife edges
legs.connect: The most sustained scrambling of the day, solid rock up to class 3.

legs.route: Mostly flat tundra ridge past Peak 5
legs.connect: Peaks 5 and 6 are tundra walking; you enter the ski area boundary at Peak 6.

legs.route: Descend a notable saddle then regain steeply
legs.connect: Drop to the low point of the traverse and climb back up.

legs.route: Tundra ridge
legs.connect: Continue along the crest.

legs.route: Steep grassy slopes after a major saddle
legs.connect: Drop about 500-600 ft to the saddle and regain it.

legs.route: Jeep road to the saddle, then the ridge
legs.connect: Follow the road to the saddle, then the ridge to the summit; this last climb feels long.

how: A ridge traverse of about 16 to 18 miles and 7,000 to 8,000 ft of gain, staying near or above 12,000 ft. The north end (Peaks 1 to 4) is the technical part, class 3 with exposed notches and a few bypasses; south of Peak 4 it is mostly tundra walking. Peaks 5, 6 and others are optional bumps on the crest, and shorter versions bail out early.
descent: From Peak 10 walk or hitch down a road toward Breckenridge, around 6 more miles. You finish in a different town from the start, so a ride or bus back to the trailhead is part of the plan.
logistics: Park at Rainbow Lake trailhead and arrange a ride or the free summer bus back from Breckenridge; allow a full day starting at dawn. Water is scarce on the ridge (mostly snowmelt, low by late summer). Winter ski area boundaries restrict travel near the south end.
notes: Mount Royal and Mount Victoria (Frisco side) are included by two of three pages as an optional start; Peak 2 is a minor summit. Distance 16 to 18 mi; gain 7,200 to 7,800 ft by source. Peak 9 and 10 elevations differ slightly between pages.

name: Apache Peak and Navajo Peak Traverse

legs.route: From the Apache/Navajo saddle or the Apache Couloir to the south ridge
West Chimney (class 4)
legs.connect: Descend Apache's south ridge, contour east around Dicker's Peck, then climb the short chimney and ledges on Navajo's west side.

how: Reach the basin below the two peaks from the lake trail, then climb to the saddle or the Apache couloir. Take Apache first, then traverse to Navajo, since the class 4 chimney is easier to climb than to downclimb. The connecting ridge has real route-finding on ledges.
descent: From Navajo, follow the east ridge toward Niwot Ridge and drop a steep gully or grassy slope to the lake trail. Some parties tag the Niwot Ridge high point on the way down.
logistics: Approach from the Brainard Lake area; a day-use fee or timed entry applies in season. The watershed boundary near Dicker's Peck is closed, so stay on the open side. Go early in summer; the chimney is a trouble spot when wet or icy.
notes: The longer Shoshoni–Apache–Navajo–Niwot traverse (14 mi, 5,000 ft, to 4th class) is described in the second source; Shoshoni–Apache passes the Chessmen towers on 3rd/4th class ledges (a search snippet says the towers are 5.9 R if climbed). Only one full page covers the Shoshoni link, so it is not a leg. Reports differ on the Apache route: couloir vs saddle.

name: Pawnee Peak and Mount Toll

legs.route: East Ridge (Little Pawnee is an optional first summit)
South slope
legs.connect: Drop to the Toll–Pawnee saddle and walk up the class 2 south slope.

how: From the Brainard Lake area, go up the Pawnee ridge (class 3 with a few short class 4 moves if you also take Little Pawnee), then cross to Toll by an easy descent and a class 2 slope. Some parties continue over Paiute toward Audubon, which is class 3 and above on Toll's north side.
descent: Drop the southeast slopes from Toll to Blue Lake (snow early in the season) and walk the lake trail out, or return to Pawnee Pass. This gives a loop instead of an out-and-back.
logistics: About 10 miles and 4,000 ft of gain for Little Pawnee, Pawnee and Toll. The Brainard Lake area needs a timed-entry or day-use fee in season. Bring traction for early-season snow on the Blue Lake descent.
notes: The 14ers report links Audubon, Paiute, Toll, Pawnee and Shoshoni in a 14.5-mile one-way loop (Paiute to Toll class 3 or 4 on the spine, rest class 1-2), a second, longer version of this link-up. Not split into a separate entry.

name: Glacier Gorge Traverse (Powell to Longs and Storm)

legs.route: Northeast Ridge (from Thatchtop, or on the way from Taylor)
Through McHenrys Notch
legs.connect: Descend into the notch by a grassy third-class ramp, then climb the featured rock on the far side.

legs.route: Long ridge, mostly third class
legs.connect: A ridge of towers, partly bypassed; roughly an hour and a half of travel.

legs.route: West Ridge bypass or northwest face
legs.connect: The hardest link, low fifth class by the bypass.

legs.route: Keyhole Route
legs.connect: Cross talus and a third-class weakness in a cliff band to join the Keyhole Route.

legs.route: Walk-off via the Keyhole saddle
legs.connect: Descend the Keyhole Route to the saddle and climb to Storm.

how: The full rim of Glacier Gorge runs from Flattop and Hallett around Otis, Taylor, Powell, McHenrys, Chiefs Head, Pagoda, Longs and Storm, about 20 miles and 12,000 ft counter-clockwise from Bear Lake. A shorter, common version starts at the Glacier Gorge trailhead over Thatchtop. Up to Powell is tundra and talus; from the notch on it is airy and technical, with low fifth class on McHenrys and Pagoda.
descent: After Storm, walk the ridge to Half Mountain and follow a trail past Mills Lake back to Glacier Gorge, or cut down to the North Longs Peak trail. This replaces the single-peak Keyhole descent with a long exit.
logistics: Needs a very early start and 13 to 15 hours for the shorter version. Water is scarce on the ridge; some is found below snow between Pagoda and Longs. Carry a rope and rappel slings if the notch holds snow or you want to rappel. Check current park rules.
notes: Sources disagree on Pagoda: northwest face 5.4, west ridge 5.7, low-5th bypass, and a 5.5 Keyhole variant; kept the highest hard grade. Other trip reports (Taylor to McHenrys sections, Chiefs Head from Black Lake) corroborate the McHenrys Notch crux. Exploring the Rockies reached only Chiefs Head, McHenrys, Powell, Taylor.

name: Chiefs Head, McHenrys, Powell and Taylor Ridge Run

legs.route: From Black Lake basin via Stone Man Pass, exposed ramp and the gendarme notch
From Stone Man Pass, up the headwall
legs.connect: Drop to Stone Man Pass and climb the ridge; about two hours.

legs.route: Through McHenrys Notch (rappels or downclimb)
legs.connect: Descend into the notch (rappels in snow years), then follow the knife edge over to Powell.

legs.route: Tundra ridge
legs.connect: Follow the tundra ridge with a short upclimb beside a snowfield.

how: A 16-mile, 14-hour partial traverse of the Glacier Gorge rim, in the direction opposite to the full counter-clockwise traverse, linking four 13ers. Chiefs Head has an exposed ramp with an awkward move above class 3. McHenrys Notch is the crux: a snowy knife edge, and a mandatory rope-down in some years.
descent: Leave Taylor by Andrews Glacier and Andrews Tarn, then down Loch Vale to the trailhead. This beats retracing the ridge.
logistics: Needs a 60 m rope and rappel slings if the notch is snowy. The glacier is a foot glissade early in the season; carry an axe. Allow a dawn start and a late return.
notes: Direction here is from one trip report; most sources run Taylor to Chiefs Head. Second source confirms the ridge order and notch crux but not this exact route. Treat as a subset of the Glacier Gorge Traverse entry. | Dropped in review: a subset of the Glacier Gorge Traverse, and its direction rests on one report.

name: Capitol–Snowmass Traverse

legs.route: Northeast Ridge (Knife Edge)
Ridge via North Snowmass, then third-class summit
legs.connect: Downclimb Capitol's southwest side, follow the ridge over gendarmes, North Snowmass and then the short crossing to Snowmass.

how: Climb Capitol by its normal route, then cross the ridge southwest to Snowmass, a 2.5 to 3 mile crest with loose rock, exposure and very dangerous gendarmes. Expect fifth-class downclimbing and climbing, with 5.5 to 5.7 sections, and bailouts at notches into Pierre Lakes basin. Going Capitol to Snowmass is easier on route-finding.
descent: Down Snowmass by the west slopes to the Lead King basin trailhead, or by the east face to Snowmass Lake and a long walk out. This ends far from where you began.
logistics: Two vehicles or a long walk back to Capitol Creek or Snowmass Creek. Carry a 60 m rope, rappel slings and a light rack. Stay apart on the ridge because of rockfall. Timing varies a lot: about 5 to 17.5 hours for the ridge itself.
notes: Grades vary by source: Capitol downclimb 5.4 to 5.7; overall rated 5.7 (R/X in one report, Grade IV). Kept highest. Exit differs: Snowmass Creek vs Lead King (Geneva Lake).
